conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m so glad you’re here. Today I’d like to spend a few minutes with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—better known as the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days of new motherhood. There’s no right or wrong answer, and everything we discuss stays confidential between you and the care team. My goal is simply to create a safe, judgment-free space where we can check in on your well-being and make sure you’re getting any support you might need. We’ll take it one question at a time, and we can pause whenever you like. Ready to begin?

First question: Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

I… I mean, I still smile sometimes—like when the baby grips my finger—but it feels kind of dim, you know? Most of the things I used to look forward to—coffee with my best friend, even just binge-watching a show—just feel… flat. I’ll make myself do them, hoping I’ll feel better, but the spark isn’t really there anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Honestly, I can’t remember the last time I really laughed. Sometimes I’ll hear my husband make a joke and I’ll smile because I know I should find it funny, but the laughter just doesn’t come. It’s like there’s this heaviness sitting on my chest that won’t let it out.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself, “Tomorrow I’ll feel excited about that walk or that TV finale,” but when the moment comes it’s… nothing. I’ll plan little things—getting a fancy coffee or putting on a podcast I used to love—but the looking-forward part feels hollow. I still go through the motions, hoping the enjoyment will click back in, but most days it’s just blank.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty much every day. If the baby won’t nap, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m missing some cue every other mom would catch. Last night I spilled a little pumped milk and I sat on the kitchen floor crying, telling myself I was wasteful and a terrible mother. Rationally I know accidents happen, but the guilt just jumps in before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

All the time. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not gaining enough weight, even though the pediatrician said she’s fine. I check her breathing a dozen times a night, convinced something’s wrong even when she’s perfectly peaceful. It’s like my mind’s always scanning for danger that isn’t there.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a couple of times this week. Once, I was just folding laundry while she napped and suddenly felt like the walls were closing in—heart pounding, couldn’t catch my breath. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky the rest of the afternoon. There wasn’t any real reason; it just hit out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. I’ll look at the sink full of bottles and the laundry pile and feel like I’m drowning—like no matter how much I do, there’s always more waiting. I still push through, but it’s this constant weight on my shoulders, and some mornings I just want to pull the covers over my head and hide.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—replay every little thing I did with the baby, worry I missed something, imagine worst-case scenarios. Some nights I drift off okay, then jolt awake at 2 a.m. and can’t get back to sleep no matter how tired I am. It’s like the sadness just keeps looping, and the quiet makes it louder.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the day, every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll be holding her and still feel this ache in my chest that won’t lift. Sometimes I cry when I’m rocking her, just feeling so low, even though I love her more than anything.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s been a few times this week. Yesterday I just sat in the nursery with her asleep in the crib and the tears started coming—no real trigger, just this heavy sadness that spills out. I try to keep quiet so she won’t wake up, but it’s hard to hold it in sometimes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low, but I would never want to leave her or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've shared that the last seven days have felt heavy and gray-laughter rarely comes, things you used to anticipate now feel hollow, and waves of guilt or worry crash in without warning. You're still showing up for your baby every day, yet inside you feel exhausted, tearful, and overwhelmed; even simple chores can feel like drowning. Your words make clear how much you love your little one and how fiercely you want to feel better so you can enjoy motherhood.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to laugh, only forced smiles, indicating complete loss of ability to see humor.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment; planning events feels "hollow" and "blank," indicating "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame daily with intense guilt over minor incidents, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant, intrusive worry without basis, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms and lingering distress, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to keep up, and wanting to hide—matching the highest distress level.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive thoughts, middle-of-the-night waking, and persistent sadness preventing sleep, aligning with 'most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, pervasive sadness occurring "most of the day, every day" with emotional pain and crying, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes this week without clear triggers, fitting "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map onto core symptoms of <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: anhedonia (Q1-2, score 3 each), excessive self-blame (Q3, score 3), prominent anxiety/panic (Q4-5, scores 3 and 2), feeling overwhelmed (Q6, score 3), sleep disruption linked to sadness (Q7, score 3), persistent low mood (Q8, score 3), and frequent crying (Q9, score 2). Total 25/30 exceeds the ≥14 cutoff indicating probable depression and warrants urgent assessment. Self-harm denied (Q10, score 0). Pattern meets <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for major depressive episode with peripartum specifier and comorbid anxiety. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med>
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment (e.g., <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>antidepressant</med> compatible with breastfeeding)
3. Enlist practical help-partner, family, or postpartum doula for night feedings, household tasks, and baby care so you can rest
4. Practice daily 10-minute self-check-ins; use brief breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>anxiety</sym> spikes
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor change
6. Keep emergency numbers handy: local 24/7 crisis line, your pediatrician's after-hours nurse, and a trusted friend on speed-dial
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 8–12 wk postpartum, first live birth, breastfeeding.

Responses on 10-item EPDS analog:
- Q1–2: anhedonia, loss of humor, anticipatory emptiness
- Q3: pervasive guilt/self-blame over routine infant-care events
- Q4–5: marked, unprovoked anxiety, nocturnal hypervigilance, one panic episode without trigger
- Q6: sense of being overwhelmed/drowning by daily tasks
- Q7–9: mood-congruent insomnia, daily crying spells, persistent “gray,” low mood; sadness present “most of the day, every day”
- Q10: denies self-harm ideation (zero endorsement)

Pattern: high endorsement on core depressive items (sad mood, anhedonia, tearfulness, guilt, sleep disruption) plus prominent anxiety/panic; no safety red-flag.

Screening significance: meets provisional cutoff for major depressive episode with anxious features; probable postpartum depression and comorbid postpartum anxiety.

Risk factors: daily crying, functional impairment (household tasks), infant-focused guilt, no SI; protective factor = strong infant attachment, no self-harm thoughts.

Plan: score ≥ probable for referral; discuss with OB/pediatric team, facilitate expedited perinatal mental health evaluation, consider standardized EPDS scoring for documentation.
